lessons.title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah
lessons.description: God as One, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge — loving and merciful — and the divine presence (Shekhinah).
lessons.content_html:
God as One: The Foundation of Jewish Belief

At the heart of Judaism lies the declaration that God is absolutely, uniquely One. Every morning and evening, observant Jews recite the Shema — a single sentence that anchors the entire tradition: “Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). This is not simply a statement of arithmetic oneness but a declaration of God’s incomparable nature. There is nothing comparable to God; no partner, no rival, no image can capture the divine reality.

This belief in monotheism distinguishes Judaism from polytheistic religions and shapes every aspect of Jewish life and practice. Because God is One, all of creation flows from a single source of will, wisdom and moral law. Jewish thinkers throughout history have emphasised that God has no body and no physical form — any description of God using human terms (such as “God’s hand” or “God’s voice”) is understood as metaphor, not literal description.

Key Fact

The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is recited twice daily by observant Jews and is the declaration of God’s absolute oneness. It is also traditionally said on the deathbed, making it both a daily affirmation and a final act of faith.

God as Creator

Jewish teaching holds that God is the Creator of all that exists. The opening words of the Torah — “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1) — establish God’s role as the ultimate originator of the universe. Creation is not a distant, mechanical event; God is intimately involved in the world God has made. Jewish theology describes God as bringing the world into existence through divine speech: “And God said, let there be light, and there was light.”

The creation narrative in Genesis 1 also establishes human dignity. Because humanity is created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim), every human being possesses inherent worth and equality. This principle underpins many of Judaism’s ethical teachings, including the sanctity of human life and the duty to protect the vulnerable.

God as Law-Giver and Judge

Judaism understands God as the ultimate source of moral law. God is not merely a powerful force but a personal God who cares how human beings treat one another. The mitzvot (commandments) — 613 of them in the Torah — represent God’s will for human conduct. These cover every area of life: prayer, food, business dealings, care for the poor, treatment of animals, and the celebration of holy days.

Jewish teaching holds that God is also the Judge of all human actions. On Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year), it is taught that God reviews the deeds of every person and writes their fate in the Book of Life. The ten days ending with Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement) are a time of deep reflection, repentance and prayer for forgiveness. Yet this God of judgement is also understood as deeply merciful: Jewish liturgy emphasises that God is “slow to anger and abounding in loving kindness.”

Jewish theology holds two divine qualities in careful balance: tzedek (justice) and chesed (loving kindness). God demands moral accountability — wrongdoing has consequences — but God also extends compassion and offers forgiveness to those who repent sincerely. The High Holy Day liturgy (the prayers of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur) is rich with both themes: God as King and Judge, and God as Father and Shepherd who does not wish anyone to be lost. This is not a contradiction but a complex portrait of a God who holds humanity to a high standard precisely because God loves humanity deeply.

The Shekhinah: The Divine Presence

One of the most distinctive and beautiful concepts in Jewish theology is the Shekhinah — the immanent presence or “indwelling” of God. The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning “to dwell.” While God is transcendent (beyond and above all creation), the Shekhinah expresses God’s nearness, the sense that God is present with and among the Jewish people.

In ancient times, the Shekhinah was associated with the Tabernacle in the desert and later with the Temple in Jerusalem. After the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, Jewish thinkers taught that the Shekhinah went with the Jewish people into exile — God was not distant from those who suffered, but accompanied them. Today, the Shekhinah is described as present whenever Jews study Torah, engage in prayer, or perform acts of justice and charity.

Students sometimes confuse the Shekhinah with a separate divine being or a lesser manifestation of God. In Jewish teaching, this is not the case. The Shekhinah is not a separate entity but a way of describing how the one, indivisible God is experienced as present and near. Jewish monotheism remains absolute: there is one God, and the Shekhinah is one way of speaking about how that single God is experienced in the world and in human life. The Shema’s declaration — “the Lord is One” — is never compromised by the concept of the Shekhinah.

Maimonides and the Principles of Faith

The medieval Jewish philosopher Maimonides (also known as the Rambam) formulated Thirteen Principles of Faith that have become widely accepted across Jewish communities. The first five concern the nature of God: that God exists, that God is one, that God has no body, that God is eternal, and that God alone is worthy of worship. These principles are summarised in a hymn called the Yigdal, sung at many synagogue services to this day.

It is worth noting that while Maimonides’ principles are widely respected, they do not function in Judaism as a formal creed in the same way the Nicene Creed functions in Catholic Christianity. Orthodox Judaism tends to treat them with great weight; Reform and Liberal Jewish thinkers may engage with them more critically, emphasising that Judaism is primarily a way of life and action rather than a system of required doctrinal belief. This reflects the broader diversity within British Jewish communities today.

Key Fact

Jewish teaching describes God as: One (echad — the Shema); Creator (borei — author of all that exists, Genesis 1:1); Law-Giver and Judge (source of the 613 mitzvot; the moral examiner on Rosh Hashanah); Loving and Merciful (chesed and rachamim in the liturgy); and Present (the Shekhinah, God’s indwelling presence among the Jewish people).
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about the nature of God in Judaism, the most common error is failing to name a source of authority. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) and Genesis 1:1 are your two strongest sources here — name them and connect them to the specific attribute you are explaining. For example: “Jewish teaching holds that God is Creator because Genesis 1:1 states that God created the heavens and the earth; this means that God is the ultimate source of all existence and that creation reflects God’s will and wisdom.” Two reasons, each developed, with at least one named source: that is the top-band structure.

On 12-mark Evaluate questions, make sure your conclusion is justified and explicit. Simply listing arguments for and against without a final reasoned judgement will cap you mid-band. End with a sentence such as: “Overall, I believe [the statement] is [supported / not supported] because [the stronger argument] and [named religious source], although those who disagree would point to [counter-argument].”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish teaching holds that God is absolutely One (the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4), the Creator of all existence (Genesis 1:1), and the Law-Giver who revealed the 613 mitzvot through Moses at Sinai.
  • God is both Judge (holding humanity accountable, especially at Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur) and deeply loving and merciful (chesed), holding justice and compassion in balance.
  • The Shekhinah describes God’s immanent presence among the Jewish people — not a separate being but God’s nearness, experienced in prayer, study and acts of justice.

Explain two ways in which the belief that God is both Just and Merciful influences Jewish life.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, both with clear explanation and development ('because...', 'this means that...'). At least one named source cited and developed (e.g. Deuteronomy 6:4 / Shema; Genesis 1:1; the Rosh Hashanah / Yom Kippur liturgy; Maimonides' Thirteen Principles). practice_questions.text:
'The most important teaching in Judaism is that God is One.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is recited twice daily and at the point of death — its centrality signals that monotheism is the foundation of all Jewish belief and practice. Maimonides lists the oneness of God as the second of his Thirteen Principles, after only God's existence. All other Jewish teachings — the covenant, the mitzvot, prayer — rest on the premise that there is one God. Arguments against: Some Jewish thinkers and communities emphasise that Judaism is fundamentally a way of life rather than a set of beliefs; observing the mitzvot (practical commandments) may be more central than any creedal statement. Others might argue that the covenant with Abraham or Moses is more foundational because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people — not merely who God is, but how God acts in history. Non-religious perspectives: A humanist might argue that ethical teachings (justice, tzedakah, Pikuach Nefesh) are more important than any theological claim, since they produce measurable good in the world. Justified conclusion required: e.g. 'The oneness of God is the most important teaching because without it every other belief loses its foundation, although the covenant and the mitzvot show how that oneness is expressed in lived Jewish experience.' Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments for and against; religious sources cited on both sides; justified conclusion present. Secure: Arguments on both sides, source cited, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One-sided or limited development; conclusion absent or weak. Emerging: Basic points, listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Rachel is a 16-year-old student attending a Reform synagogue in Leeds. Her rabbi explains that the Shekhinah is present whenever Jews study Torah together. Explain two reasons why the concept of the Shekhinah might be important to Rachel and her community.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per reason identified, 1 mark for each reason developed. Example answers: The Shekhinah offers comfort — it teaches that God is not distant but present with the community, especially during times of difficulty (e.g. when studying or praying together after a period of loss). The Shekhinah encourages communal worship and Torah study — knowing that God's presence is found where Jews gather motivates regular attendance at the synagogue and engagement with sacred texts.

lessons.title: Life After Death and the Messiah
lessons.description: Olam ha-ba, resurrection and judgement; the Messiah in Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.
lessons.content_html:
Jewish Beliefs About Life After Death

Unlike some other religious traditions, Judaism does not place enormous emphasis on detailed doctrines about life after death. The Tenakh focuses primarily on this world — on how to live justly, on the covenant relationship with God, and on the communal life of the Jewish people. Nevertheless, Jewish teaching does hold that this life is not all there is, and several important concepts address what lies beyond death.

The most significant term is olam ha-ba — “the world to come.” This refers to a future state of existence in which the soul continues after the death of the body. Some Jewish thinkers describe it as a realm of pure spiritual existence; others connect it to a future messianic age when the world is restored and the dead are resurrected. In the Talmud, the world to come is described as the place where righteous souls experience closeness to God.

Key Fact

Jewish teaching on life after death centres on three ideas: the soul’s continued existence in olam ha-ba (the world to come); judgement by God according to deeds in this life; and, in many traditions, a future resurrection of the body when the Messiah comes. These beliefs vary across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.

Judgement and Resurrection

Jewish teaching holds that God judges human beings according to their deeds. The annual pattern of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur mirrors this: on Rosh Hashanah, God opens the Book of Life and reviews the deeds of every person; on Yom Kippur, the judgement is sealed. The idea of judgement motivates ethical living — knowing that actions matter to God and have consequences beyond this life.

Belief in the resurrection of the body is held particularly strongly within Orthodox Judaism. Maimonides included belief in resurrection as one of his Thirteen Principles of Faith. The resurrection is understood as God’s ultimate vindication of the righteous: those who suffered unjustly in this world will be restored. Orthodox Jewish morning prayers include the declaration “Blessed are You, Lord our God, who restores life to the dead.”

Orthodox Judaism affirms both the existence of the soul in olam ha-ba and the physical resurrection of the body. These are held as literal beliefs, supported by Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles and traditional prayer texts. Orthodox communities regard resurrection as a core tenet.

Reform Judaism tends to emphasise the immortality of the soul rather than physical resurrection. Some Reform thinkers interpret resurrection metaphorically — as the enduring influence of a good life rather than a literal bodily rising. Reform prayer books have sometimes modified traditional resurrection language to speak instead of spiritual continuity. The focus in Reform communities is often on creating a just world in this life (tikkun olam) rather than detailed beliefs about the next.

Liberal Judaism (particularly the UK Liberal movement, founded 1902) generally takes a more open and questioning approach. Many Liberal Jews understand afterlife concepts symbolically, emphasising that goodness and righteousness have their own reward and that the details of olam ha-ba are beyond human certainty. What matters is living ethically and in accordance with Jewish values now.

The Messiah (Moshiach)

The concept of the Moshiach (Messiah) is one of the most distinctive elements of Jewish belief. The Jewish understanding of the Messiah is significantly different from the Christian one: in Jewish teaching, the Messiah is not a divine being but a human leader — a great king descended from the line of King David — who will usher in an era of universal peace, justice and the knowledge of God.

The Hebrew prophets — especially Isaiah — describe a future age in which swords will be turned into ploughshares, the nations will live in peace, and the Jewish people will return to the land of Israel. The Messiah is the agent through whom God will bring about this transformation. Maimonides lists belief in the eventual coming of the Messiah as his twelfth Principle of Faith, stating that even if the Messiah delays, one must wait for his arrival.

Orthodox Judaism awaits the coming of a personal Messiah — a specific individual who will fulfil all the biblical criteria: rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem, gathering all Jews to the land of Israel, and bringing an era of universal peace. This is understood literally and is a central hope in Orthodox prayer and liturgy.

Reform Judaism has generally reinterpreted the concept, moving away from the idea of a personal Messiah towards a “messianic age” — a future era of justice, peace and human flourishing that the entire Jewish people (and indeed all humanity) helps to bring about. Rather than waiting for one individual, the responsibility lies with all people to pursue justice and repair the world (tikkun olam).

Liberal Judaism similarly tends to understand the Messiah symbolically — as a vision of a better world that inspires ethical action now, rather than a prophetic prediction of a single future individual. Both Reform and Liberal traditions emphasise that Judaism’s deepest calling is to work for justice in the present world.

Key Fact

Orthodox Judaism awaits a personal moshiach (Messiah) descended from King David, who will rebuild the Temple and bring universal peace. Reform and Liberal Judaism tend to reinterpret this as a “messianic age” brought about through human action and tikkun olam — rather than through one individual.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about Jewish beliefs on life after death or the Messiah, you must name a sacred source. Strong choices are: the Tenakh (e.g. the Psalms, the prophets Isaiah or Ezekiel on resurrection); Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles of Faith (twelfth principle — belief in the Messiah; thirteenth — belief in resurrection); or the Talmud’s description of olam ha-ba. You also need to name the sub-tradition: Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism hold different views, and the mark scheme rewards this contrast. A top-band answer might read: “Orthodox Judaism holds that belief in the resurrection of the body is a core tenet, as stated by Maimonides in his Thirteen Principles of Faith; this means that death is not the end but that God will restore the righteous at the end of days.”

On 12-mark Evaluate questions about the Messiah, remember: the arguments ‘for’ a personal Messiah are Orthodox in nature; the arguments ‘against’ may draw on Reform/Liberal reinterpretation AND on non-religious/humanist views that reject any supernatural intervention in history. Your justified conclusion must say which argument is stronger and WHY — not just describe both sides.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish teaching on life after death centres on olam ha-ba (the world to come), divine judgement, and (in Orthodox tradition) physical resurrection; Reform and Liberal Judaism emphasise the soul’s immortality and ethical living now over detailed afterlife doctrines.
  • The Messiah (moshiach) in Jewish teaching is a future human leader descended from King David, who will bring universal peace and justice — not a divine figure; Orthodox Judaism awaits a personal Messiah; Reform and Liberal traditions focus on a messianic age achieved through tikkun olam.
  • These contrasts between Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism are exactly what the exam rewards — always name the sub-tradition when explaining Jewish views on afterlife and the Messiah.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the coming of the Messiah is the most important Jewish belief.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Maimonides lists belief in the Messiah as his twelfth Principle of Faith, stating that one must wait for the Messiah even if he delays — indicating its centrality to Orthodox Jewish theology. The messianic hope runs through the entire Hebrew prophetic tradition (Isaiah, Ezekiel) and through daily Orthodox prayer. It provides hope and direction for the entire Jewish people. Arguments against: Judaism is primarily a way of life and action rather than a system of beliefs; observing the mitzvot, keeping Shabbat, upholding tikkun olam may be more central to Jewish identity than any particular theological doctrine. Reform and Liberal Jews re-interpret or de-emphasise the personal Messiah — yet they are fully committed Jews. The Shema's declaration of God's oneness might be argued as the single most important belief. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that the concept of a Messiah is a human projection of the desire for a better world, and that the real work of repair is the responsibility of each individual, not a future leader. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced arguments for and against, Jewish sources on both sides, non-religious view included, justified conclusion present. Secure: Arguments both sides, source cited, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One-sided; conclusion absent or weak. Emerging: Basic, listing, no conclusion.

lessons.title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land
lessons.description: The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3), the Covenant at Sinai, Moses and the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17).
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Covenant?

A covenant is not a simple contract. It is a solemn, binding relationship — in the Jewish context, an agreement between God and the Jewish people that carries profound obligations and promises on both sides. The covenants at the heart of Jewish theology are not merely ancient historical events; Jewish teaching holds that they remain active and binding today. They define who the Jewish people are in relation to God and what God expects of them.

Two covenants stand at the foundation of Jewish belief: the covenant with Abraham (recorded in Genesis 12 and 17) and the covenant at Sinai (recorded in Exodus 20), sealed through the giving of the Torah and the Ten Commandments.

The Covenant With Abraham

In Genesis 12:1-3, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland and travel to a land that God will show him. The promise is threefold: land (“the promised land”), descendants (a great nation), and blessing (through Abraham’s descendants, all the families of the earth will be blessed). This is one of the most important passages in the Tenakh because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people and holds out a universal vision — Abraham’s family becoming a source of blessing for the entire world.

The covenant with Abraham was renewed and developed in Genesis 17, where God gives Abraham the sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) as the physical mark of the covenant. Every Jewish male circumcised at eight days old carries the sign of this covenant in his body — making it an embodied, communal identity marker across all generations.

Key Fact

The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) contains three promises: a land (Canaan, the “promised land”); descendants (a great nation); and blessing to all peoples of the earth through Abraham’s family. These promises form the bedrock of Jewish identity and hope.

Moses and the Covenant at Sinai

Moses is the most significant human figure in the Torah. After leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, Moses ascended Mount Sinai and received God’s revelation. The covenant made at Sinai is qualitatively different from the covenant with Abraham: at Sinai, the entire Israelite people — not just one individual and his family — entered into a binding agreement with God. They would be God’s people; God would be their God. In return, they accepted the Torah and its commandments as their way of life.

The significance of Moses cannot be overstated. He is described in the Torah as the greatest of all prophets — the only person who spoke with God “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jewish teaching holds that no prophet would arise in Israel greater than Moses, and his role as the transmitter of the Torah — both written and oral — makes him the founding teacher of the Jewish tradition.

The Ten Commandments

The Ten Commandments (Decalogue) recorded in Exodus 20:1-17 are the most prominent and widely recognised part of the Sinai revelation. They divide into two groups: the first four concern the relationship between humanity and God (no other gods; no idols; not taking God’s name in vain; keeping Shabbat holy), and the remaining six concern the relationship between people (honour your parents; do not murder; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not give false witness; do not covet).

Jewish tradition teaches that the full covenant at Sinai involved not just the Ten Commandments but the complete Torah — 613 commandments covering every aspect of life. The Ten Commandments are understood as a summary or foundational statement rather than the entirety of divine law. In synagogue services, the Ten Commandments are recited on certain occasions, and many synagogues display them on plaques near the ark.

The Torah divides the 613 mitzvot into two broad categories. Mitzvot between man and God (bein adam l’Makom) include prayer, observing Shabbat and festivals, keeping dietary laws, and daily rituals of study and gratitude. These sanctify the individual’s relationship with the divine. Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l’chavero) include not stealing, not lying, caring for the poor, and treating every person with dignity. These sanctify communal life. Jewish teaching holds that, for the mitzvot between man and man, God’s forgiveness on Yom Kippur cannot substitute for making direct amends to the person wronged.

The “promised land” (Eretz Yisrael) has remained a central element in Jewish consciousness throughout history, even during centuries of exile. Orthodox communities typically understand the promise of the land as literal and ongoing. Some Orthodox Jews make aliyah (immigration to Israel) as a religious act, fulfilling the covenant. Reform and Liberal communities hold more varied views: many affirm a spiritual or cultural connection to the land of Israel without prioritising physical settlement as a religious obligation. It is important to note that these are internal Jewish theological debates — the exam expects you to describe what different Jewish traditions teach, not to adjudicate the political dimensions.

Key Fact

Two foundational covenants: (1) Abraham — Genesis 12:1-3: land, descendants, blessing for all peoples. Sign: Brit Milah (circumcision). (2) Sinai — Exodus 20:1-17: the entire Israelite people accept God’s Torah and commandments; God becomes their God. Moses is the mediator. Together these covenants define Jewish identity and obligation.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about the covenant, you have two excellent sources ready: Genesis 12:1-3 (the covenant with Abraham) and Exodus 20:1-17 (the Ten Commandments at Sinai). Use them precisely. For example: “The Covenant with Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3 is important because God promised Abraham both land and descendants, meaning that Jewish identity is tied to a specific people and a specific place, giving Jews a sense of purpose and mission across all generations.” Two developed reasons, at least one named source: that is top-band structure.

On 12-mark Evaluate questions about the relative importance of the two covenants, remember: ‘which is more important’ arguments need to weigh them against each other. The Abraham covenant is more personal and promises; the Sinai covenant is more communal and demands. Both sides should use named sources. Your conclusion must explain WHY one side is stronger.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) promises land, descendants and blessing for all peoples; the physical sign is Brit Milah (circumcision). It establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people.
  • The Covenant at Sinai (Exodus 20:1-17) extends the covenant to the entire Israelite people, through Moses; the Ten Commandments and the full Torah are accepted as God's law for all of Jewish life.
  • The 613 mitzvot divide into duties to God (bein adam l'Makom) and duties to other people (bein adam l'chavero); both categories are considered binding obligations, not optional guidelines.

practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Abraham Covenant is the oldest and most foundational — it establishes the identity of the Jewish people as God's chosen people and promises them a land and a future (Genesis 12:1-3). Without Abraham there is no Sinai — the covenant with Abraham creates the people who will later receive the Torah. The physical sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) makes it an embodied, lifelong commitment. Arguments against: The Sinai covenant encompasses the whole people, not just one individual and his family; it gives the Jewish people their entire way of life through the Torah and the 613 mitzvot, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17). Jewish daily life is structured around the Sinai covenant — prayer, Shabbat, festivals, dietary laws all flow from it. Moses — the mediator of the Sinai covenant — is the greatest of all Jewish prophets. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that neither covenant is literally true but that the ethical teachings they generated (justice, care for the poor, respect for life) are what matter. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments; sources on both sides; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source present, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. lessons.title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
lessons.description: Justice, tikkun olam, tzedakah and chesed; the sanctity of life and Pikuach Nefesh; the 613 mitzvot and free will.
lessons.content_html:
Jewish Moral Principles: An Overview

Judaism is often described as a religion of action. Beliefs matter deeply, but what Jewish teaching emphasises above all else is how people treat one another and how they respond to God’s call to live justly. The mitzvot are not experienced by most Jews as burdensome restrictions but as a framework of sanctity — a way of bringing holiness into every moment of daily life. Jewish tradition teaches that no mitzvah is too small to matter: even feeding a hungry person or speaking honestly in a business deal is an act of worship.

Four core moral principles run through Jewish ethical teaching and appear explicitly in the Torah and the prophetic tradition: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity) and chesed (loving kindness). These four principles operate together and are reflected in countless practical mitzvot.

Tzedek: Justice

The Hebrew word tzedek means both “justice” and “righteousness.” The Torah commands, “Justice, justice shall you pursue” (Deuteronomy 16:20) — the double repetition of the word signals its urgency. Jewish courts (batei din) have a long tradition of applying Torah law to resolve disputes fairly. The prophets of the Tenakh — particularly Amos, Micah and Isaiah — repeatedly challenged the wealthy and powerful to treat the poor justly, warning that God is not satisfied with ritual worship when justice is absent from public life. “Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

Tzedakah: Charity as Obligation

Tzedakah is often translated as “charity” but the Hebrew root is tzedek (justice) — giving to the poor is understood not as an act of generosity but as an act of justice. The poor have a right to a portion of the community’s resources; the wealthy have an obligation to give. Many Jewish communities have a tzedakah box (pushke) in the home into which small amounts are placed regularly, making giving a habitual part of daily life. Organisations such as World Jewish Relief operate from this principle, providing aid to vulnerable people across the world regardless of religion.

A common error is to describe the 613 mitzvot as “rules Jews have to follow.” Jewish teaching frames the mitzvot very differently: they are not restrictions imposed from outside but a gift from God — a detailed guide to living a sanctified life. Observant Jews describe the sense of meaning and structure the mitzvot bring to daily life. Keeping Shabbat is not experienced as a ban on work; it is experienced as a weekly gift of rest and family togetherness. This is the texture the exam rewards: mitzvot as joyful duties and expressions of the covenant, not as arbitrary rules.

Tikkun Olam: Healing the World

The concept of tikkun olam — repair or healing of the world — has become one of the most widely cited principles of Jewish ethics in the modern period, particularly in Reform and Liberal communities. It expresses the idea that the world as it is is not as it should be: there is suffering, injustice and brokenness. Every act of justice, every act of tzedakah, every act of chesed is a stitch in the repair of the world. Modern Jewish organisations that campaign for human rights, environmental justice or refugee support often invoke tikkun olam as their motivating principle. Jewish Care and HIAS (the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society) are examples in Britain and internationally.

The Sanctity of Human Life and Pikuach Nefesh

One of the most distinctive and powerful teachings in Judaism is Pikuach Nefesh — the principle that preserving human life takes precedence over almost all of the commandments. The Talmud teaches that to save a single life is as if one has saved an entire world (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9). This remarkable teaching reflects the absolute sanctity of every human being, created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim).

In practice, Pikuach Nefesh means that if a life is at risk, a Jew is obligated to break Shabbat rules, eat non-kosher food, or disregard almost any other commandment in order to save that life. Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews all affirm this principle, though they may apply it differently in edge cases. Medical professionals in the Jewish community may work on Shabbat; an ambulance driver who is Jewish will drive to save a life. The principle shows that the mitzvot serve human life — they are never more important than life itself.

Key Fact

Pikuach Nefesh: preserving human life overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot. Rooted in the teaching that every person is created in God’s image (tzelem Elohim) and that “one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world” (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9). This principle is accepted across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.

Free Will and the Mitzvot

Jewish teaching holds that God gave human beings genuine free will. The mitzvot are binding obligations, but no one is compelled to observe them. The Torah presents the choice explicitly: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse; therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). The fact that God requires observance of the mitzvot but does not compel it makes every act of obedience or disobedience morally significant.

The tension between free will and divine commandment is one that Jewish thinkers have explored across the centuries. If God knows in advance what each person will choose, how is that choice truly free? Maimonides wrote that “free will is given to every human being” and that God’s foreknowledge does not remove human moral responsibility — a teaching maintained across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism today.

Chesed — loving kindness — is expressed in countless ways in British Jewish community life. A large Reform synagogue in north-west London runs a weekly food bank and visits housebound elderly members; the young people’s group at a Manchester Reform synagogue organises clothing collections for asylum seekers. These acts are understood not simply as “volunteering” but as performing a mitzvah — fulfilling a divine commandment to show kindness to others. The distinction matters: chesed is not optional generosity but a religious obligation rooted in the covenant relationship with God.

Key Fact

The four core Jewish moral principles: Tzedek (justice — pursue fair treatment for all); Tikkun olam (repair the world — act to reduce suffering and injustice); Tzedakah (charity — giving as a moral obligation, not optional generosity); Chesed (loving kindness — showing compassion to all, especially the vulnerable).
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On 6-mark Explain questions about Jewish moral principles, your most powerful sources are: Deuteronomy 16:20 (“Justice, justice shall you pursue”) for tzedek; Talmud Sanhedrin 37a (“one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world”) for Pikuach Nefesh; and Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) for free will. You must name at least one of these and develop your reason around it.

A very common error is describing tzedakah as “voluntary charity.” Always clarify that tzedakah is a mitzvah — a moral obligation, not optional generosity. The Hebrew root of tzedakah is tzedek (justice): giving to the poor is not above-and-beyond kindness but what justice requires. This distinction often marks the difference between Developing and Mastering band answers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jewish moral life is structured around four core principles: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity as a moral obligation, not optional), and chesed (loving kindness).
  • Pikuach Nefesh — preserving human life — overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot; rooted in the Talmudic teaching that saving one life is equivalent to saving an entire world (Sanhedrin 37a).
  • The mitzvot are understood not as restrictive rules but as a framework of holiness; God gave human beings free will, making every act of obedience or kindness morally meaningful.

Sub-tradition application adds depth: e.g. how Reform synagogues organise food banks as a community mitzvah. Secure: Two reasons present, source cited but not fully developed. practice_questions.text:
'Pikuach Nefesh is the most important moral principle in Judaism.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Pikuach Nefesh overrides almost every other mitzvah — if life is threatened, even Shabbat rules, dietary laws and festival restrictions may be set aside. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 37a) states that saving one life is equivalent to saving an entire world, indicating its supreme priority. It reflects the foundational belief that every person is created in tzelem Elohim (Genesis 1:27). Arguments against: Other principles such as tzedek (justice) and tikkun olam underpin the entire structure of Jewish social ethics and affect every interaction in daily life, not just emergency situations. One could argue that the Shema — declaring God's absolute oneness — is more foundational because it defines who God is, on which all other teachings rest. Some might argue that the covenant itself (the relationship between God and the Jewish people) is the most important moral framework. Non-religious view: A humanist might affirm Pikuach Nefesh's content (the supreme value of human life) while rejecting its religious basis. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed; sources on both sides; non-religious view; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source cited, conclusion. Developing: One side; weak conclusion. Emerging: Listing, no conclusion.
